subject: biology-hl
about: Original practice questions written for NevaIB from the IB guide's syllabus understandings and the school's unit order. Not IB past-paper questions, not publisher material and not IB markschemes: the marking points are written for self-marking. Organisms, experiments and data in data-response items are invented for practice.

choices: All the organisms of different species living in one area
All the members of a species throughout the world at any time
Members of one species living in the same area at the same time
A group of species that interact in a food web
items.note: A community is all the interacting populations of different species in an area.

items.stem: Quadrat sampling is suitable for estimating the population size of:
choices: Fast-moving animals such as deer
Sessile organisms such as plants
Birds that migrate each year
Fish in a large lake
items.note: Quadrats suit organisms that do not move. Mobile animals need capture–mark–release–recapture.

items.stem: The carrying capacity of an environment is:
choices: The number of species living in it
The rate at which a population grows
The minimum population size needed to avoid the species becoming extinct
The maximum population size it can support sustainably
items.note: Limited resources (food, space, water) set the carrying capacity, K.

items.stem: 40 snails are marked and released. Later, 50 are captured, of which 8 are marked. The estimated population is:
An assumption of capture–mark–release–recapture is that:
choices: Marked individuals are easier to catch
The population changes size between samples
Marks fall off some animals before the second sample is taken
Marked individuals mix randomly with the population
items.note: Also: marking does not harm or affect behaviour, and there is no significant birth, death or migration between samples.

items.stem: In a sigmoid population growth curve, the transitional phase occurs because:
choices: Limiting factors start to reduce the growth rate
Birth rate rises sharply as resources become more plentiful
Death rate falls to zero
Immigration stops completely
items.note: As density rises, competition for resources, predation and disease increase, slowing growth until K is reached.

items.stem: A relationship in which both species benefit is:
choices: Parasitism
Mutualism
Predation
Competition
items.note: E.g. root nodules with Rhizobium, zooxanthellae in corals. Parasitism benefits one at the other's expense.

choices: A forest fire caused by lightning
An unusually cold winter
Spread of an infectious disease
A volcanic eruption
items.note: Disease spreads faster when individuals are crowded. Weather events and disasters act regardless of density.

items.stem: Predator and prey populations often cycle, with predator peaks lagging behind prey peaks, because:
choices: Predators and prey reproduce at exactly the same time
Prey numbers depend only on the weather
Predators eat other predators when prey numbers rise
Predator numbers rise only after prey are plentiful, then fall after prey decline
items.note: Abundant prey → more predator offspring → prey decline → predator decline (lag due to reproduction time).

items.stem: A chi-squared test for association between two plant species in quadrats gives χ² = 6.2 with 1 degree of freedom (critical value at p = 0.05 is 3.84). The conclusion is:
choices: Reject the null hypothesis: there is a significant association
Accept the null hypothesis: the species are distributed independently
The result is not significant because 6.2 is less than 3.84
No conclusion can be drawn from χ² tests
items.note: χ² > critical value → the difference between observed and expected is unlikely to be chance (p < 0.05).

choices: A plant forming a mutualism with nitrogen-fixing bacteria
A predator controlling the population of its prey
Release of chemicals by a plant that inhibit other plants nearby
Competition for light between members of the same plant species
items.note: E.g. black walnut releasing juglone. A chemical form of competition.

items.stem: Outline how to estimate the population size of a plant species in a field using random quadrats.
markscheme: Use random numbers to place quadrats (coordinates on a grid) (1)
Count the number of individuals in each quadrat (1)
Calculate mean per quadrat and multiply by (total area ÷ quadrat area) (1)
items.tactic: Random sampling: say how randomness is achieved and how you scale up.

items.stem: Explain why an invasive species can cause a decline in native species.
markscheme: No natural predators/pathogens in the new area, so the population grows rapidly (1)
May prey on, or transmit disease to, native species (1)
items.tactic: Link the lack of controls to the effects on natives.

items.stem: Distinguish between top-down and bottom-up control of a community, with an example of each.
markscheme: Top-down: population controlled by consumers/predators at a higher trophic level (1)
Example, e.g. sea otters controlling sea urchins (kelp forests) (1)
Bottom-up: controlled by availability of resources/producers at lower levels (1)
Example, e.g. nutrient supply limiting phytoplankton and the food chain above it (1)
items.tactic: Definitions plus a named example for each.

items.stem:
(Invented data for practice.) Presence of two invented plant species in 100 quadrats: both 38; species A only 12; species B only 10; neither 40.
(a) Calculate the expected number of quadrats with both species if they are distributed independently. (b) State the null hypothesis. (c) The χ² value is 31.4 (critical value 3.84, 1 degree of freedom). State and explain the conclusion. (d) Suggest an ecological reason for the result.
markscheme: (a) A present in 50 quadrats, B in 48 (1)
(b) There is no association between the distributions of A and B (they are independent) (1)
(c) 31.4 > 3.84, so reject the null hypothesis: positive association (38 observed vs 24 expected) (1)
(d) Both prefer the same abiotic conditions, or one benefits the other (e.g. shelter) (1)
items.tactic: Unfamiliar context: find the syllabus idea being tested, quote the data (with units) when you describe a trend, then explain it with that idea. One marking point per linked step.
